title: Skills, Memory, and Agent Harnesses Are the Next AI Platform Layer
author: Dr. Hernani Costa
summary_short: Reusable skills, governed memory, and audited harnesses form the next AI platform layer for European scale-ups. Skills replace ad-hoc prompts; memory replaces raw context with a policy-governed store; the harness logs every tool call. Together they produce one evidence package for EU AI Act conformity assessments and DORA third-party risk reports.
summary_medium: The chat-interface era of AI agents is ending. The next platform layer is reusable skills, governed memory, and audited execution harnesses — three components that together turn experimental toys into operational tools. Skills are named, versioned capabilities stored in a registry; memory is the policy-governed subset of context an agent reads and writes across sessions; the harness is the execution layer that enforces access control, rate limits, and structured audit logs on every invocation. The article frames a five-level maturity model from prompt chaos up to fully audited harness, and a 30-day adoption path that catalogs the first twenty skills in week one, pilots controlled memory with privacy review in weeks two and three, and produces the first compliance report from harness logs in week four. For European scale-ups, the same three artefacts — skill registry, memory policy, harness log — satisfy EU AI Act Article 16 technical documentation, DORA Article 28 third-party risk reporting, and EDPB-aligned GDPR Article 30 records of processing without re-derivation. The article also names four operational failure modes: skill-registry sprawl past two hundred entries, harness bypass under shipping pressure, memory poisoning through indirect injection, and absence of a documented purge cadence.
summary_long:
The chat-interface era of AI agents is ending. The next platform layer is reusable skills, governed memory, and audited execution harnesses — three components that together turn experimental toys into operational tools, and for European scale-ups, they double as the compliance evidence package that EU AI Act Article 16 and DORA Article 28 are about to require.

Skills are named, versioned, reusable capabilities. Each lives in a git-tracked catalog — typically YAML or TypeScript, one file per skill — with an owner, the tools it may call, input and output schema, and test fixtures. Skills replace scattered prompts the same way web frameworks replaced raw PHP files around 2008 to 2012: structure produces reliability.

Memory is the controlled subset of context an agent reads and writes across sessions. It has a documented retention policy, a scope boundary (user-level versus session-level), and a privacy review process aligned with GDPR Article 30 and EDPB guidance. Memory typically lives in a PostgreSQL table or a vector store with per-record retention timestamps and scope keys; the policy that governs reads and writes lives in the same git repository.

The harness is the execution and audit layer — usually under one thousand lines of code — that wraps the model call, the skill registry, and the memory store, and emits a structured audit log per invocation. It enforces access control, rate limiting, and an MCP server allowlist; it is the primary defence against prompt injection because it controls tool invocation independently of the prompt.

The maturity model has five levels: L0 prompt chaos, L1 prompt library, L2 reusable skills, L3 governed memory, L4 audited harness. The 30-day adoption path moves a team from anywhere on that ladder to L4. Days 1 to 7: the CTO and platform engineering lead catalog twenty skills in a versioned registry. Days 8 to 21: the AI transformation lead with security and privacy leads ships a controlled-memory pilot; the pilot must pass privacy review with memory operations logged and reversible. Days 22 to 30: the operations leader and procurement-aware engineering manager wire the harness and generate the first compliance report from harness logs.

Without budget approval, a platform engineering lead can take five concrete first-week actions: inventory every production prompt via codebase grep, rewrite the top three highest-traffic prompts as named YAML skills, add per-invocation structured logging, run OpenSSF Scorecard against the new skill repository, and sketch the memory policy on one page. Day seven produces evidence the security lead and procurement-aware engineering manager can review.

Four named failure modes apply. Skill-registry sprawl past two hundred entries without a deprecation policy becomes a parking lot; the mitigation is a quarterly retirement review for skills with zero invocations in ninety days. Harness bypass — engineers route around the harness for a quick fix; the mitigation gates model-API credentials behind the harness service and tracks direct-call counts. Memory poisoning through indirect injection — an agent retrieves a document containing instructions telling the model to write an elevated-trust record; the mitigation namespaces memory writes by agent identity and never lets the model decide whether a record is authoritative. Memory without a documented purge cadence is a discovery liability waiting for a regulator request.
